name: Augustus
summary: Augustus ended the civil wars and built a monarchy in republican dress, keeping the Senate and magistracies while holding the army and decisive powers himself. He presented his rule as a restoration of ancestral custom, backing it with religious revival, marriage and morals laws, and a permanent professional army. He expanded the empire widely but left advice to keep it within existing limits.

sources.title: Augustus
sources.author: Wikipedia
sources.usedFor: Standing army, praetorians, vigiles, marriage laws, proscriptions, imperial cult

property-fundamental.rationale: He took part in the proscriptions and land confiscations of the civil wars, but in the Res Gestae he claims he was the first to pay for lands assigned to veterans, buying estates in Italy and the provinces.

cut-welfare.rationale: Suetonius quotes his own writing that he was inclined to end the grain distributions because dependence led farmers to neglect agriculture, yet he kept and funded them (Res Gestae lists his grain distributions); the evidence points both ways.

strong-leader.rationale: Suetonius reports he twice considered restoring the republic but concluded it would be dangerous to leave the state in the hands of more than one man, so he kept it; the Res Gestae presents his settlement as ending civil war.

state-harmful.rationale: He built up state institutions on a large scale (army, guard, fire and police services, treasury, road network) and ruled as their head.

empower-police-military.rationale: He created a standing professional army, the Praetorian Guard, the urban cohorts and the vigiles (fire and watch), and endowed a military treasury with his own money for soldiers' gratuities.

traditional-family.rationale: He personally drove the marriage and morality legislation (the Julian marriage law and the later Papia Poppaea law, with penalties for the unmarried and childless and rewards for parents, and the law against adultery) to strengthen marriage and family life.

more-religion-public.rationale: He rebuilt 82 temples in Rome, built or restored many more, revived neglected rites (Lupercalia, Secular Games, Compitalia, augury of Safety), and increased the number, privileges and income of priests.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: In the Res Gestae he states that by new laws he restored many ancestral traditions that were falling out of use; he also revived old rites and festivals and ordered the toga worn in the Forum.

gradual-change.rationale: He states in the Res Gestae that he refused any office offered to him that was contrary to ancestral custom, and he kept republican forms and magistracies while concentrating power in himself.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: He avoided the titles of king, dictator and lord and framed his rule as a restored republic, while building a de facto hereditary principate; the evidence points both ways.

political-violence-never.rationale: In the Res Gestae he says he raised an army at nineteen to free the republic from a faction, exiled his father's killers and then defeated them in war, and he later proscribed his opponents.

separate-church-state.rationale: He held the chief priesthood (pontifex maximus) himself together with other priestly offices while ruling, and ran state religion as part of the state, with public games, vows and sacrifices decreed by the Senate.

military-superiority.rationale: He boasts of conquests, of forcing the Parthians to return Roman standards and seek friendship, and of embassies from distant kings; Roman power over all rivals was his stated achievement.

ethnic-nation.rationale: Inferred: his stated aim, as reported by Suetonius, was to keep the Roman people unmixed with foreign or servile blood by restricting citizenship grants and manumission, which does not amount to an ethnic definition of the nation.

duties-before-rights.rationale: His marriage and morals laws imposed duties on citizens to marry and have children, with penalties for evasion, placing the community's needs ahead of individual choice.

limit-population.rationale: His marriage laws aimed to raise the number of citizen births, with rewards for children and penalties for the childless, the opposite of limiting population.

restore-past-order.rationale: He presented his rule as a restoration of the republic and of ancestral custom, reviving old rites, dress and moral norms; this is his own framing in the Res Gestae and Suetonius's account of his measures.

harm-principle.rationale: He legislated private morals and conduct for adults through laws on extravagance, adultery and chastity, and marriage, and regulated dress and seating, which goes beyond preventing harm to others.

national-rebirth.rationale: Inferred: he presented his regime as restoring ancestral customs falling into disuse and held the Secular Games, a ceremony marking a new age, but he described a restoration, not a radical rebirth.

territorial-expansion.rationale: The Res Gestae records that he extended the frontiers of all provinces bordering unconquered peoples and added Egypt, Pannonia and others; Tacitus reports that his last written advice recommended keeping the empire within its present limits, so late evidence points the other way.

rule-by-example.rationale: He set up statues of Rome's great men so that rulers would measure up to them and says he set precedents for posterity, but he also legislated heavily on morals with penalties; the evidence points both ways.

national-self-determination.rationale: He conquered and annexed many peoples, though in some cases (Armenia, per the Res Gestae) he preferred to hand the kingdom to a client king instead of making it a province; the king was one he chose.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Suetonius reports he took omens and dreams seriously and feared thunder, carrying a sealskin as protection; he did not rely on reason alone.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: The Res Gestae records that he restored eighty-two temples, the Capitol, Pompey's theatre and the aqueducts and completed his father's buildings; Suetonius says he left Rome in marble.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: He legislated seating that kept women to the upper rows at shows and had his daughter and granddaughters taught spinning and weaving, and his marriage laws treated women's status in terms of marriage and children; none of this is a statement about public roles.

night-watchman-state.rationale: He greatly extended the state: grain distributions, public building, aqueducts, roads, fire brigades, a state military treasury and legislation on marriage, dress and morals.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: He legislated rank and status distinctions: citizenship granted sparingly, limits on manumission, separate seating by order, and marriage restrictions between orders, so equality before the law was not his policy.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Inferred: the Res Gestae grounds his authority in the Senate's and people's unanimous consent and in oaths taken by all Italy and the provinces, suggesting he regarded consent as a source of legitimacy.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: As a triumvir he pressed the 43 BC proscriptions, which outlawed hundreds of senators and knights without trial; Suetonius says he was more insistent than his colleagues that no one be spared.

head-commands-forces.rationale: The armies swore their oath to him, he commanded the legions through his own deputies (legati) and set up the Praetorian Guard, and he appointed the prefects and provincial governors who ran the imperial provinces.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: He held thirteen consulships and renewed his tribunician power year after year; he declined a consulship for life and an annual and perpetual one, so his acceptance of repeated and extended office was limited.

people-in-arms.rationale: He replaced the citizen levies and warlords' private armies of the civil wars with a professional standing army with fixed terms of service and a military treasury to pay veterans.

death-penalty.rationale: He carried the 43 BC proscriptions through with notable severity and his regime executed conspirators, while in ordinary trials he is described as lenient; he did not renounce capital punishment.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Inferred: Suetonius says he granted citizenship sparingly to keep the people free of foreign or servile blood, which favours descent-based membership, though Roman citizenship by descent was already normal.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: He directed the aediles to forbid anyone appearing in the Forum except in the toga, scolding crowds in dark cloaks, which enforces conformity to ancestral custom.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Rather than curbing religious institutions he increased the number and importance of priests and their allowances and privileges, especially the Vestals, though he also took the chief priesthood into his own hands and culled prophetic books.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Inferred: he says he freed the republic from the tyranny of a faction and accepted the title Father of the Country by acclamation of Senate, knights and people, presenting himself as head of the whole community.

sacred-ruler.rationale: He took the title 'son of the deified' Julius and was named Augustus; a law made his person sacred and his name was put in the Salian hymn, but he refused to be called lord, refused temples in Rome and accepted provincial worship only jointly with Rome.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: In the Res Gestae he claims he held no more power than his colleagues in any magistracy and refused powers contrary to ancestral custom; Suetonius adds that he wanted even his friends bound by the same laws, though his actual power was far wider than this claim.

leader-cult.rationale: He accepted honours such as the title Father of the Country, a golden shield and the name Augustus, yet he removed about eighty silver statues of himself from Rome, refused to be called lord and checked public flattery, so the evidence points both ways.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: By order of the people and Senate he increased the number of patricians, and he kept rank-based privileges such as reserved seating for senators and knights; he kept hereditary orders in being rather than abolishing them.

elective-rulers.rationale: He arranged his own succession by adoption and family designation (Gaius and Lucius, then Tiberius) instead of leaving the choice of ruler to election, although Senate and people formally acclaimed his offices.

parliament-supreme.rationale: In the Res Gestae he says he transferred the republic to the Senate and people and held no more power than his colleagues, yet he held tribunician power and wide imperium and personally drove major legislation; the evidence points both ways.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: The Res Gestae lists his payments to the people, soldiers and the treasury from his own patrimony, and Suetonius says he raised the property rating of impoverished senators and urged prominent men to adorn the city.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: Suetonius says that when he found the spirit of his marriage law being evaded by frequent changes of wife he set a limit on divorce.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: He founded a state military treasury, funded by his own money and by taxes on inheritance and sales, to pay gratuities to veterans, a pay-as-you-go style state scheme for soldiers, not a statement on pensions generally.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: He passed laws against extravagance, razed an overly lavish villa built by his granddaughter and, per Suetonius, kept a simple household and gave away the palace furniture of Alexandria.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: His marriage legislation gave privileges and rewards to married citizens with children and penalised celibacy; Suetonius records him raising the rewards when the knights resisted, and he displayed Germanicus's children as an example.

non-intervention.rationale: The Res Gestae lists his installing and replacing kings in Armenia, Parthia and Media, receiving royal suppliants and annexing Egypt.

public-access-to-information.rationale: Suetonius lists among his innovations that the proceedings of the Senate should no longer be published.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: The Res Gestae boasts that Parthian kings sent their sons as pledges, that kings sought refuge with him as suppliants and that distant peoples sent embassies seeking friendship; Suetonius adds he demanded oaths and hostages.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Suetonius records both severity (the proscriptions, exile of his daughter and granddaughter, disbanding guilds) and notable leniency toward critics and libellers; the evidence points both ways.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: He instead built a permanent army of 28 legions, with auxiliaries and a military treasury, and kept it for the whole of his rule.

dynastic-succession.rationale: He groomed his grandsons Gaius and Lucius as successors and, after their deaths, adopted Tiberius and Agrippa Postumus; succession to him was arranged within the family by adoption rather than by birth to a child.

term-limits.rationale: He refused a lifelong consulship but held the consulship thirteen times and held the tribunician power continuously for decades, so the evidence points both ways.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: He launched wars of conquest in Spain, the Alps, Pannonia, Germany, Arabia and Ethiopia, which he lists as achievements in the Res Gestae, though Suetonius says he claimed never to wage war without just cause.

arms-reduction.rationale: After the civil wars he cut the army from about 60 legions to 28 and settled over 300,000 soldiers in colonies or towns; the reduction was to a standing force he judged adequate, not to disarmament.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Suetonius reports he suppressed armed gangs and footpads who went about with swords, put guards in place, inspected landowners' workhouses and disbanded illegal guilds.

premarital-sex.rationale: His law on adultery and chastity criminalised adultery and illicit sex with women of citizen status, and he banished his daughter Julia and later his granddaughter Julia for misconduct.

national-church-status.rationale: Suetonius says he respected ancient, well-established foreign rites but despised other foreign cults, and he favoured the traditional state cult with funding, temples and priests; this is not an explicit statement about legal status.

notes: His own Res Gestae presents his rule as a restored republic; the Suetonius and Tacitus reports are secondhand. The Tacitus report of his advice to keep the empire within its frontiers is the only evidence against expansion and Tacitus himself hedges on its motive.
